references.text: David's battle against Goliath illustrates the principle of assessing one's chances against a superior enemy. In [ref:1 Sam 17:1-54|1 Samuel 17:1-54], David goes to war with trust in God, despite seemingly insurmountable odds.

[ref:Ordsp 20:18|Proverbs 20:18] emphasizes that plans should be made with wise counsel and that war should be waged with good strategy—the same principle of carefully assessing the situation before acting that Jesus teaches in the parable.

[ref:Ordsp 24:6|Proverbs 24:6] states that with wise leadership one can wage war, and victory comes through many counselors. This reflects Jesus' point about carefully considering one's resources before going to war.

In [ref:1 Kong 20:11|1 Kings 20:11], the king of Israel warns against boasting before the battle is decided. The principle is the same: one should carefully assess the outcome before committing oneself.

The preceding parable about the tower builder in [ref:Luk 14:28-30|Luke 14:28-30] carries the same message: one must calculate the cost beforehand. Both parables serve as illustrations of what it takes to be a disciple of Jesus.

[ref:Luk 14:33|Luke 14:33] gives the conclusion to both parables: whoever does not give up all that they own cannot be a disciple of Jesus. The parable about the king assessing war points forward to this requirement of total surrender.

In [ref:2 Kong 18:19-25|2 Kings 18:19-25], the Assyrian king confronts Hezekiah with the question of whom he trusts when rebelling—a practical illustration of having to assess one's resources against a superior enemy.

In [ref:2 Krøn 25:17-24|2 Chronicles 25:17-24], Amaziah ignores Joash's warning and goes to war without carefully assessing the situation, leading to disaster. This illustrates the consequences of not following the principle Jesus describes.
